title: Web Apps with Azure App Service
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain what Azure App Service runs for you, how a request reaches your code, and what stays your job.
- Choose an App Service plan tier, and decide when to scale up and when to scale out.
- Configure an app with app settings and release it safely through a deployment slot and a swap.
- Compare App Service with virtual machines, Azure Container Apps and Azure Static Web Apps for a given workload.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Friday, 21:40. Dewi is still in the office. Since Lunch 09 the storefront runs on two virtual machines behind a load balancer, and it survived its first server failure without a single lost sale. The price is her Friday nights: patch Ubuntu on one VM, take it out of the pool, update Python, renew the certificate, restart nginx, put it back, repeat on the other one. "I'm a developer," she sighs, "and I spend more time looking after servers than writing the checkout."

On Monday, Ibu Sari adds a second worry. Harbolnas, Indonesia's 12.12 online shopping day, is eight weeks away. Last year the traffic peak lasted about four hours, and she doesn't want to pay all year for servers sized for one evening. Dewi also wants to release a new checkout page before the sale, without taking the shop offline to do it.

Today's question: can Azure run the web servers for us, grow them for the sale, and let Dewi ship new code with no downtime?

Reading

1. Platform as a service for web apps

In Lunch 06 you rented a virtual machine and became responsible for everything above the hardware: the operating system, the language runtime, the web server, security patches and the scaling plan. Azure App Service moves that line. It is a platform as a service (PaaS) for HTTP workloads: websites, REST APIs and mobile back ends. Microsoft runs and patches the operating system, the language runtimes and the web front ends; you bring code and configuration. You still own your data, your users' access, your app's settings and, of course, your bugs. The shared-responsibility slider from Lunch 02 has moved one big step to the right.

App Service runs .NET, Java (Java SE, Tomcat and JBoss), Node.js, Python and PHP on Windows or Linux. Python runs on Linux only. If your stack isn't on the list, or you already package the app as an image, App Service also runs a custom container. The platform knows each built-in stack: when Dewi deploys Python code, App Service can install the packages from requirements.txt and start the app with Gunicorn, a production web server, without her writing a startup script.

How does a request reach the code? Each Azure region runs App Service on large groups of servers. Front ends take every incoming request for your app's address, such as app-nusa-ab12c.azurewebsites.net or www.nusantararetail.co.id. (Apps created in the portal get a longer default name that includes a random part and the region, so nobody outside your organization can ever recreate it.) They terminate TLS, decide which instance should handle the request and forward it. Workers are the virtual machines that run your code; the ones reserved for you form your App Service plan. Your deployed files live on shared storage, so any of your workers can start your app. A separate deployment endpoint (the SCM site, also known as Kudu) accepts new code from the CLI, from GitHub Actions or from the portal.

You never sign in to those workers to patch them. When a new Python or Ubuntu patch is out, the platform rolls it out. When a worker's hardware fails, the platform moves your app to a healthy one. That is the trade: you give up control over the machine, and in return the whole night shift of server care disappears.

The trade has edges you should know before you move a workload. Your app is reachable over HTTP and HTTPS only, not on arbitrary ports, so a service that listens on its own TCP port belongs elsewhere. You can't install operating-system packages into the built-in stacks; if the app needs them, build a custom container. Work that runs for hours in the background doesn't belong in a web request: App Service has WebJobs for background tasks, and Lunch 14 introduces Azure Functions for event-driven jobs. And the platform can't fix a slow database query, a memory leak or a password committed to Git. Those stay yours.

Tip: TLS ends at the front ends, so your code receives plain HTTP plus an X-Forwarded-Proto header that says whether the visitor used HTTPS. Don't write your own HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect: switch on the HTTPS Only setting and let the front ends do it.

2. App Service plans: the compute you pay for

Every app runs in an App Service plan. The plan defines the region, the operating system, the pricing tier, the instance size and the number of instances. Several apps can share one plan, and then they share its instances: the storefront and the staff admin portal could sit on the same two workers. Apps in a plan scale together, because scaling changes the plan, not the app.

That gives the most important billing rule of this lunch: you pay for the plan, not for the apps. In the dedicated tiers, each instance is billed per hour whether the apps on it are busy, idle or stopped. The Free tier is free, with strict limits. The tier also decides which features you get:

Tier | Compute | Max instances | Autoscale | Deployment slots | Custom domain with TLS | Typical use
Free (F1) | Shared, 60 CPU minutes a day | 1 | No | No | No (azurewebsites.net only) | Learning, quick demos
Shared (D1) | Shared, Windows only | 1 | No | No | No TLS for custom domains | Tiny hobby sites
Basic (B1–B3) | Dedicated | 3, manual | No | No | Yes | Dev/test, small production sites
Standard (S1–S3) | Dedicated | 10 | Yes | 5 per app | Yes | Most production web apps
Premium v3 and v4 | Dedicated, faster hardware, memory-optimized options | 30 | Yes | 20 per app | Yes | Busy production, larger apps
Isolated v2 | Dedicated, inside your own virtual network (App Service Environment v3) | 100 | Yes | 20 per app | Yes | Strict network isolation, very large scale

The numbers are the published limits at the time of writing (October 2026); check the App Service limits page before you design around them. Two rows deserve a second look for Nusantara Retail. Basic has dedicated compute but no deployment slots and no autoscale. Standard is the first tier with both, which is why it's the usual starting point for a production shop.

There are two ways to get more power:

- Scale up (vertical): move the plan to a bigger size or a higher tier, for example from S1 to S2 or to P1v3. Each instance gets more CPU and memory, or the plan gains features. You don't redeploy anything, though the apps restart.
- Scale out (horizontal): add instances of the same size, for example from one to three. You can do it by hand (Basic and up), with autoscale rules that react to metrics such as CPU or to a schedule (Standard and up), or, on Premium v2, v3 and v4 plans, with automatic scaling, where the platform decides based on HTTP traffic.

How do you pick a size? Start small, measure CPU and memory under realistic load, then adjust; changing the tier later takes minutes, not a migration. Development and test environments can share one Basic plan. Production deserves its own plan, so that a busy test run can't slow the shop down. A plan that runs all year can be bought at a discount with reservations or the Azure savings plan for compute (Lunch 19 compares the options). In regions with availability zones (Lunch 03), higher tiers can also spread a plan's instances across zones, so one zone failure doesn't close the shop; check which tiers and minimum instance counts zone redundancy needs in your region.

Scale out only works smoothly if the app is stateless. If Dewi's code kept shopping carts in the memory of the web server process, a shopper whose next request lands on another instance would see an empty cart. State belongs in a database or a cache (Lunches 11 and 12). App Service can pin a browser to one instance with an affinity cookie, but that's a crutch, not a design.

Warning: Stopping a web app does not stop the bill. The plan's instances keep running and keep being charged until you scale the plan down to the Free tier or delete it. In the labs, delete the whole resource group.

3. Getting code in and configuration right

Deploying means getting a build of your code onto the workers. App Service offers several routes, and they all end at the same deployment endpoint:

Option | How it works | Use it when
az webapp up | One command that creates the group, plan and app, zips the current folder and deploys it | You want a quick first deployment. Azure CLI 2.87 (June 2026) formally deprecated it; it still runs
az webapp create + az webapp deploy | You create the resources explicitly, then upload a zip package. With SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT=true, App Service installs your dependencies | Scripts, labs and simple pipelines
GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines | Every push builds, tests and deploys, ideally to a staging slot | Team development and repeatable releases
Deployment Center | A portal page that connects a repository and writes the workflow for you | Your first CI/CD setup, without writing YAML
Container image | App Service pulls an image from Azure Container Registry or another registry | You already ship the app as a container

What happens to a Python zip package after upload? If build automation is on, App Service's build system creates a virtual environment and runs pip install for everything in requirements.txt. When the app starts, the Linux container looks for a Django project (wsgi.py) or a Flask app in app.py or application.py and starts Gunicorn for it. Anything unusual, such as a FastAPI app, needs a startup command in the general settings. If it finds nothing, it serves a default page, which is a common surprise after a deployment from the wrong folder.

Configuration is the other half of a release. The same storefront code should run as the real shop in production and as a test shop in staging, so values that differ between environments live outside the code:

- App settings are name–value pairs that App Service hands to your code as environment variables when it starts. Dewi's Python code reads os.environ["STORE_NAME"]. Changing a setting restarts the app, so the new value takes effect within seconds.
- Connection strings are a separate list for database connections, also exposed as environment variables (with a prefix that names the database type).
- Key Vault references let a setting point at a secret in Azure Key Vault instead of holding the secret. The value looks like @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...), and the app's managed identity reads the real secret. Nobody needs to paste a password into the portal again (Lunch 15).
- General settings pick the runtime version, the startup command, HTTPS Only, the minimum TLS version, Always On (Basic and up), which keeps the app loaded between requests, and a health check path.

When something goes wrong, App Service gives you several windows into the app. The log stream shows what the app writes to its console, live, in the portal or with az webapp log tail. Diagnose and solve problems runs ready-made checks for crashes, slow responses and configuration mistakes. Application Insights records every request, dependency call and exception for later analysis; Lunches 16 and 30 go deeper.

4. Deployment slots and swaps

Deploying straight into production has two problems. While the instances restart and warm up with the new code, the first customers get slow answers or errors. And if the new code is broken, every customer sees it at once, and the "undo" is another deployment.

A deployment slot solves both. A slot is a live app with its own host name, for example app-nusa-ab12c-staging.azurewebsites.net, that runs in the same plan on the same instances as production. Slots come with Standard (5 per app) and Premium and Isolated (20 per app). They cost nothing extra, but they do use some of the plan's CPU and memory. Dewi deploys version 2 to the staging slot, tests it on its own address while customers keep buying through version 1, and then asks App Service to swap staging into production:

Production keeps serving the old code until every staging instance has restarted with production's settings and answered a warm-up request. Only then does App Service switch the routing, so no request is dropped. If finance spots a bug half an hour later, Dewi swaps again: the previous version is still deployed in the staging slot, so it is warmed up and switched back in a minute or two, with no redeployment and no downtime. For extra caution, a swap with preview pauses after the settings step so you can test staging with the production configuration before you complete the swap.

What travels with the code during a swap, and what stays with the slot? App settings and connection strings travel, unless you mark them as deployment slot settings (often called sticky settings). That is how staging keeps its own test database connection: mark it sticky, and it never ends up in production. Some things always stay with the slot, including custom domain names, TLS certificates, HTTPS Only, scale settings, access restrictions and managed identities. Slots can also take a share of live traffic, such as 10 percent of shoppers, for testing a change on real users before a full swap. One Linux detail: auto swap, which swaps automatically after every deployment to a slot, is available for Windows apps only.

Here's how Dewi could plan the new checkout for Harbolnas. On Monday, the pipeline deploys version 2 to staging. On Tuesday, the team tests the staging address and then routes 10 percent of real shoppers to it for a day. On Wednesday night, well before the sale, Dewi swaps and watches the error rate. If anything looks wrong, she swaps back within a minute. During the sale itself nobody deploys anything: the safest release is the one you finish early.

5. Domains, security and networking at a glance

The storefront needs its own name and an HTTPS padlock, and the admin portal must not be open to the whole internet. App Service has a building block for each:

Feature | Direction | What it gives you | Tiers
HTTPS Only and minimum TLS version | Inbound | Redirects HTTP to HTTPS and refuses old TLS versions | All
Custom domain with a managed certificate | Inbound | www.nusantararetail.co.id with a free, auto-renewed certificate (not wildcard) | Basic and up
Built-in authentication | Inbound | Sign-in with Microsoft Entra ID, Google, GitHub and others before any request reaches your code | All
Access restrictions | Inbound | Allow or deny traffic by IP range, service tag or subnet | All
Private endpoint | Inbound | A private IP address in your virtual network; public access can be switched off | Basic, Standard, Premium
Virtual network integration | Outbound | The app can reach private resources, such as a database behind a private endpoint | Basic and up
Managed identity | Outbound | The app gets its own Entra ID identity to call Key Vault, Storage or SQL without secrets | All

Built-in authentication, often called "Easy Auth", is handy for the staff-only admin portal: with a few settings, everyone must sign in with their Nusantara Retail account before the first page loads. Access restrictions could allow the admin portal only from head office's public IP address, or allow the storefront only through Azure Front Door (Lunch 27). Private endpoints and virtual network integration come back in Lunch 25. You don't need all of these on day one, but it helps to know that each problem already has a switch.

6. App Service or something else? Nusantara Retail's choice

App Service isn't the only place to run a website in Azure. Here's how it compares with its neighbours:

| Virtual machines | App Service | Container Apps | Static Web Apps
You manage | OS, runtime, web server, patches, scaling design | Code, settings, plan size and count | Container images, scale rules | Front-end code and small APIs
You deploy | Software installed on a VM | A code package or a container | A container image (as revisions) | Static files built from a Git repository
Scaling | Scale sets (Lunch 23) | Instances in a plan, autoscale | Replicas from zero upwards with event-driven rules | Content served from many locations worldwide, automatically
You pay for | VM hours and disks | Plan instances (Free tier for learning) | Resources used per second, or dedicated workload profiles | A free plan or a paid Standard plan
Pick it when | You need full OS control or legacy software | You host web apps and APIs on a supported stack | You run microservices, background workers or event-driven containers | You publish single-page apps and static sites
Nusantara example | A legacy service that syncs the stores' POS terminals | The storefront and the admin portal | Inventory and recommendation microservices (Lunch 13) | The 12.12 promotion microsite

Three questions settle most cases. Do you need control of the operating system, or software that only installs on a server? Then use a VM. Is there no server-side code at all? Then Static Web Apps is simpler and cheaper. Is the workload a set of containers that should scale independently, possibly down to zero? Then look at Container Apps. For a classic web app or API on a supported language, App Service is usually the shortest path to production.

For the storefront, the choice is App Service on Linux with the Python stack. In production, Nusantara Retail would use at least the Standard tier with two or more instances for availability, an autoscale rule for Harbolnas, a staging slot for every release, HTTPS Only with a managed certificate on www.nusantararetail.co.id, and Key Vault references for secrets. Customer data must stay in Indonesia, so production would run in Indonesia Central (Jakarta), after checking that the chosen tier is offered there. The labs use Southeast Asia, where every tier is available.

Moving the web tier doesn't move the data. The product database still sits on the old server next to the pantry, and that's next lunch's job: Azure SQL, in Lunch 11. Later lunches add containers (13), serverless functions for the order pipeline (14) and a global front door with a web application firewall in front of App Service (27).

Pause and think: Dewi's current code keeps each shopper's cart in a Python dictionary inside the web server process. What happens to a cart when autoscale adds a second instance, and what happens when Dewi swaps a new version into production? Where should the cart live instead?

Field notes from Stefanus

Rehearse the undo button before you need it. The first swap I run on a new production app is a rehearsal, not a release: I put a harmless change in staging, swap it into production, swap it straight back and time both moves. That proves to the team that rollback really works, and it flushes out the settings that should have been sticky while the stakes are still low. Two habits make the rehearsal easy. Every app I deploy shows its version and the instance that served the request on a small page, so after a swap or a scale-out I see facts instead of guessing. And before a big sale I write down who may press Swap and what makes them press it, because a rollback that waits for a meeting is no longer quick.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: Azure App Service plans (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/app-service/overview-hosting-plans) — how plans are billed, how apps share them and how to scale them.
- Microsoft Learn: Set up staging environments in Azure App Service (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/app-service/deploy-staging-slots) — every step of a swap, sticky settings and traffic routing.
- Microsoft Learn: Configure a Linux Python app for Azure App Service (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/app-service/configure-language-python) — the build, the startup command and the log stream for Python apps.

quiz.q: The storefront and the admin portal share one Standard S1 plan with two instances. To save money over the weekend, Dewi stops the admin portal app. How much does the bill drop?
quiz.a: It doesn't drop at all. You pay for the plan's instances, and stopping one app leaves both instances running. To save money, scale the plan in or down, or move the admin portal to a cheaper plan.

quiz.q: Ibu Sari wants zero-downtime releases through a staging slot and automatic scaling for Harbolnas, at the lowest possible price. Which is the lowest tier that offers both?
quiz.a: Standard (for example S1). It's the first tier with deployment slots (five per app) and autoscale; Basic has dedicated instances but neither feature.

quiz.q: After a swap, the production storefront starts writing orders into the test database. What went wrong, and how do you prevent it?
quiz.a: The database connection string wasn't marked as a deployment slot setting, so it travelled with the code during the swap. Mark environment-specific settings as slot settings so that they stay with their slot.

quiz.q: Rizky, the contractor, put the database password in app.py. Dewi moves it to an app setting. The security lead suggests a Key Vault reference instead. Why is that better still?
quiz.a: With a Key Vault reference, the secret lives only in Key Vault, where access is controlled, logged and rotated; the app reads it with its managed identity. An app setting holds the secret itself, so anyone who can read the app's configuration can read the password.

quiz.q: Marketing's 12.12 promotion microsite is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript generated by a static site tool. They want it fast for shoppers all over Indonesia and as cheap as possible. App Service, Container Apps or Static Web Apps?
quiz.a: Static Web Apps: it serves static files from many locations close to the visitors, has a free plan and creates preview environments for pull requests. There is no server-side code to host, so App Service would be overkill.

takeaways: App Service is PaaS for web apps and APIs: Microsoft runs the OS, the runtimes and the TLS-terminating front ends; you own the code, the settings, the data and who gets access.
You pay for the App Service plan (tier × size × instances), not for the apps. Stopping an app doesn't stop the bill, and Free F1 is for learning only.
Scale up for bigger instances or more features; scale out for more instances. Deployment slots and autoscale start at the Standard tier, and scaling out needs a stateless app.
App settings become environment variables; secrets belong in Key Vault references; environment-specific values should be sticky slot settings.
Deployment slots let you test on production hardware and swap with no downtime, and swapping back is a quick rollback that needs no redeployment.

lab.title: Move the storefront to PaaS
lab.text:
What you'll build

Nusantara Retail's storefront moves off its virtual machines and onto Azure App Service. You deploy the provided Python (Flask) storefront to a Linux App Service plan on the Free (F1) tier, configure the store name as an app setting, force HTTPS, and watch the app's log stream. Then you break the configuration on purpose, read the logs to find out why, and fix it. In the optional stretch you scale the plan to Standard (S1), deploy version 2 to a staging slot and swap it into production without downtime.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)).
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. Nothing to install.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings and this lab's names:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/10-app-service
source ../common/config.sh
source lab.env
echo "Group: $RG   Plan: $PLAN   App: $APP   Runtime: $RUNTIME"

Important: The Free tier costs nothing, but the stretch goal uses a Standard plan that is billed per hour while it exists. Finish with the Clean up section, even if you stop halfway. Opened a new Cloud Shell session? Run the three lines starting with cd, source and source again so the variables come back.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–6 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Meet the app and create the resource group

Before you hand code to a platform, know what the code expects. This storefront needs one setting, STORE_NAME, and shows which instance and host name served each request.

ensure_rg "$RG" 10
sed -n '1,14p' app/app.py          # the docstring explains the settings the app reads
cat app/requirements.txt           # Flask and Gunicorn: App Service installs these for you
az webapp list-runtimes --os-type linux --output table | grep -i python

The last command lists the Python versions App Service offers on Linux. You should see PYTHON:3.12 among them. If a newer Azure CLI shows a different layout, look for the 3.12 line anyway. If 3.12 has gone, pick a listed version, run export LAB10_RUNTIME="PYTHON:3.13" (for example) and source lab.env again.

Checkpoint: the group exists and carries the lab tags: az group show --name "$RG" --query "{name:name, location:location, lunch:tags.lunch}" --output table

Task 2 · Deploy with one command

az webapp up is the shortest path from a folder of code to a running web app. It creates the plan and the app, turns on build automation, zips the current folder and deploys it. It must run from the folder that contains the code. Expect 3–6 minutes, most of it while App Service installs Flask and Gunicorn.

cd app
az webapp up \
  --name "$APP" \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --plan "$PLAN" \
  --location "$LOCATION" \
  --runtime "$RUNTIME" \
  --sku F1
cd ..

While it runs, read what it is doing: it creates the plan asp-nusa-<suffix> on the Free tier (always Linux for Python apps, so there's no operating system to choose), creates the web app with the Python stack, enables the SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT build setting, uploads a zip of the folder and prints a summary. On the server, the build system (Oryx) creates a virtual environment and installs requirements.txt; then App Service finds app.py and starts it with Gunicorn. az webapp up also saves your choices in app/.azure/config so that a second run in the same folder needs no parameters.

Note: Azure CLI 2.87 (June 2026) formally deprecated az webapp up. It still works and prints a yellow warning. Scripts should use the explicit commands below, which is what solution.sh does. If your CLI no longer has az webapp up, use these instead:

az appservice plan create -g "$RG" -n "$PLAN" --location "$LOCATION" --is-linux --sku F1 --output none
az webapp create -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --plan "$PLAN" --runtime "$RUNTIME" --output none
az webapp config appsettings set -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --settings SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT=true --output none
mkdir -p "$OUT_DIR"
(cd app && python3 -m zipfile -c "$OUT_DIR/storefront-v1.zip" app.py requirements.txt)
az webapp deploy -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --src-path "$OUT_DIR/storefront-v1.zip" --type zip

Now read the app's host name from Azure (new apps can get a longer, unique host name, so don't guess it) and call the health endpoint:

HOST=$(az webapp show -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --query defaultHostName --output tsv)
echo "https://$HOST"
curl -s "https://$HOST/health"; echo

Don't open the home page yet: it needs the setting you add in Task 3. (If you're curious and open it anyway, you get a polite error page. That is on purpose; you'll see why in Break it and fix it.)

Tip: Prefer the portal? Create a resource › Web App: Publish Code, Runtime stack Python 3.12, Operating System Linux, your region, Pricing plan Free F1 › Review + create. Then deploy the code with the explicit az webapp deploy commands from the note above and continue with Task 3.

Checkpoint: curl prints ok, and az webapp show -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --query "{state:state, host:defaultHostName}" --output table shows Running.

Task 3 · Configure the store with an app setting

App settings are name–value pairs that App Service passes to your code as environment variables. The same code can then run as the Kemang store in production and as a test store in staging, with no code change. Changing a setting restarts the app, so give it about 30 seconds.

az webapp config appsettings set -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --settings "STORE_NAME=${STORE}" --output none
az webapp config appsettings list -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --query "[].name" --output tsv

You should see STORE_NAME and SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT. Now open https://$HOST in your browser: the page shows the store name, Version 1.0, the instance that served you and the host name.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Open the web app › Settings › Environment variables › App settings › + Add, enter STORE_NAME, select Apply, then Confirm the restart. Anyone who can read the app's configuration can read these values, so never put passwords here: Lunch 15 replaces secrets with Key Vault references.

Checkpoint: curl -s "https://$HOST/" | grep -o "$STORE" prints Nusantara Retail - Kemang.

Task 4 · Force HTTPS

App Service terminates TLS at its front ends, and every app gets a certificate for its azurewebsites.net name. Plain HTTP still works until you switch on HTTPS Only, which redirects every http:// request to https://.

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "http://$HOST/"                       # probably 200: plain HTTP is allowed
az webapp update -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --https-only true --output none
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} -> %{redirect_url}\n" "http://$HOST/"    # now a 301 redirect to https://
az webapp config show -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --query minTlsVersion --output tsv    # 1.2 or higher

Tip: Prefer the portal? Settings › Configuration › General settings: set HTTPS Only to On and check Minimum inbound TLS Version.

Checkpoint: az webapp show -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --query httpsOnly --output tsv prints true, and the second curl shows 301 -> https://....

Task 5 · Watch the log stream

When something goes wrong in production, the first place to look is what the app itself writes. App Service collects the container's console output; the log stream shows it live.

az webapp log config -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --docker-container-logging filesystem --output none
az webapp log tail -g "$RG" -n "$APP"

Leave it running and refresh the storefront in your browser a few times. Within about 30 seconds you see lines such as INFO [storefront] Served the home page for Nusantara Retail - Kemang (version 1.0, instance ...), mixed with platform messages about the container. Press Ctrl+C to stop streaming.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Monitoring › Log stream shows the same output. Diagnose and solve problems is the next stop when the log isn't enough.

Checkpoint: at least one [storefront] Served the home page line appeared in the stream.

Task 6 · See what you are paying for

Your app runs on the plan, and the plan is what you pay for. Look at it.

az appservice plan show -g "$RG" -n "$PLAN" \
  --query "{tier:sku.tier, size:sku.name, instances:sku.capacity, linux:reserved}" --output table
az webapp list-instances -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --query "[].name" --output tsv

The Free tier runs your app on shared infrastructure with a daily CPU quota of 60 minutes, one instance, no custom domains, no deployment slots, no autoscale and no SLA. That is perfect for learning and useless for the 12.12 sale. In the portal, open the plan's Scale up (App Service plan) page to compare what each tier adds, without changing anything.

Checkpoint: the table shows tier Free, size F1, one instance and linux = True.

Break it and fix it

Someone "tidies up" the configuration and deletes a setting they didn't recognise. Do it yourself:

az webapp config appsettings delete -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --setting-names STORE_NAME --output none
sleep 45                                                     # the app restarts after a settings change
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "https://$HOST/"

Symptom: the page answers 500, and the browser shows "Sorry, the shop is having a moment." The page gives customers no details, which is deliberate. Find the cause the way an engineer would: start the log stream with az webapp log tail -g "$RG" -n "$APP", refresh the page, and read the ERROR line.

Hint and fix

The log says Required app setting STORE_NAME is missing. Put the setting back and wait for the restart:

az webapp config appsettings set -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --settings "STORE_NAME=${STORE}" --output none
sleep 30 && curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" "https://$HOST/"     # 200 again

Two lessons: keep error pages generic for customers but specific in your logs, and treat configuration as part of the release (in Lunch 20 it becomes code). In production you would also alert on a rise in HTTP 5xx responses (Lunch 16).

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This deletes the resource group rg-lunch10-<suffix> (the plan, the web app and any slot) and removes the local files in ~/lab10-out and app/.azure. Nothing is created outside the resource group. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
Yellow warning that az webapp up is deprecated | Azure CLI 2.87 and later mark the command as deprecated | Expected. The command still works; or use the explicit commands in the Task 2 note
Website with given name app-nusa-… already exists. | Web app names are global and yours is taken | export LAB10_APP="app-nusa-${SUFFIX}2", then source lab.env and repeat Task 2
This region has quota of 0 instances for your subscription. Try selecting different region or SKU. | Some trial and student subscriptions have no App Service quota in a region | Run cleanup.sh, export LOCATION=eastasia (or another region), source both files again and restart the lab
The browser shows the App Service default Python page, not the storefront | The code wasn't deployed, or App Service couldn't find app.py | Run Task 2 again from inside the app folder; check that app.py and requirements.txt are at the root of the zip
:( Application Error page | The container failed to start | Run az webapp log tail and look for a Python traceback; Diagnose and solve problems helps too
"Sorry, the shop is having a moment." (HTTP 500) | STORE_NAME is missing or empty | Run the Task 3 command again
Error 403 - This web app is stopped. | The app was stopped, or the Free tier used its 60 CPU minutes for the day | az webapp start -g "$RG" -n "$APP", or wait for the daily quota to reset
az webapp log tail shows nothing | Logging is off, or nobody has visited the site yet | Run the az webapp log config command, wait 30 seconds and refresh the page
Creating the staging slot fails | Deployment slots need the Standard tier or higher | Scale the plan to S1 first (stretch step 1)
curl: (6) Could not resolve host | $HOST is empty, usually in a new Cloud Shell session | Source both files again and re-run the HOST=$(...) line from Task 2

Stretch goals

A zero-downtime release with a staging slot (, about 15 minutes). Deployment slots start at the Standard tier, so you pay for an S1 instance while it exists.

1. Scale the plan up and create the slot, copying production's settings. HTTPS Only belongs to each slot and never travels in a swap, so set it on the slot too:
  az appservice plan update -g "$RG" -n "$PLAN" --sku S1 --output none
  az webapp deployment slot create -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --slot staging --configuration-source "$APP" --output none
  az webapp update -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --slot staging --https-only true --output none
  az webapp config appsettings set -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --slot staging --settings SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT=true --output none

2. Build version 2.0 from a copy of the code and deploy it to the slot only:
  rm -rf "$OUT_DIR/v2" && mkdir -p "$OUT_DIR/v2" && cp app/app.py app/requirements.txt "$OUT_DIR/v2/"
  sed -i 's/^APP_VERSION = "1.0"/APP_VERSION = "2.0"/' "$OUT_DIR/v2/app.py"
  (cd "$OUT_DIR/v2" && python3 -m zipfile -c "$OUT_DIR/storefront-v2.zip" app.py requirements.txt)
  az webapp deploy -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --slot staging --src-path "$OUT_DIR/storefront-v2.zip" --type zip

3. Test the slot on its own host name. Production still shows Version 1.0:
  STAGING_HOST=$(az webapp show -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --slot staging --query defaultHostName --output tsv)
  curl -s "https://$STAGING_HOST/" | grep -o "Version [0-9.]*"
  curl -s "https://$HOST/" | grep -o "Version [0-9.]*"

4. Swap. To see that no request fails, open a second Cloud Shell session (the Open new session button) and start a poller there first:
  cd ~/azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/10-app-service && source ../common/config.sh && source lab.env
  HOST=$(az webapp show -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --query defaultHostName --output tsv)
  for i in $(seq 1 60); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} " "https://$HOST/"; sleep 2; done

  Then, in the first session:
  az webapp deployment slot swap -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --slot staging --target-slot production
  curl -s "https://$HOST/" | grep -o "Version [0-9.]*"      # Version 2.0

5. Roll back by running the same swap again: Version 1.0 returns after a short warm-up, with no redeployment.

More ideas

- On S1, scale out to two instances with az appservice plan update -g "$RG" -n "$PLAN" --number-of-workers 2, then run curl -s "https://$HOST/" | grep -o 'instance</dt><dd>[^<]*' a few times. Requests without a session cookie can land on either instance.
- Give App Service a health check path so it can take a sick instance out of rotation: az webapp config set -g "$RG" -n "$APP" --generic-configurations '{"healthCheckPath": "/health"}'.
- Fork the repository and connect Deployment Center to GitHub Actions, so every push to main deploys.

Challenge brief

Build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep):

1. A resource group rg-lunch10-<suffix> in your lab region.
2. A Linux App Service plan asp-nusa-<suffix> (the Free F1 tier is enough).
3. A web app app-nusa-<suffix> with the Python 3.12 stack, running the code in app/.
4. An app setting STORE_NAME with your store's name; https://<host>/ returns HTTP 200 and shows that name.
5. HTTPS Only switched on.

Optional: a staging slot on a Standard plan, with version 2.0 swapped into production (verify.sh reports it as a note). Then run bash verify.sh. Stuck? Peek at solution.sh or switch to Guided mode.
